legacy: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was one of the greatest astrophysicists of the twentieth century. His work transformed humanity's understanding of stars, stellar evolution, black holes, and the physical structure of the universe. His theoretical predictions shaped modern astrophysics and provided foundations for much of contemporary cosmology. The Chandrasekhar Limit remains one of the most important concepts in astronomy and is essential to understanding the life cycle of stars.
earlyLife: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was born in Lahore, British India (now Pakistan). He was the nephew of Nobel Prize-winning physicist C. V. Raman. From an early age he demonstrated extraordinary mathematical talent and a passion for science. He studied physics at Presidency College in Madras before earning a scholarship to the University of Cambridge, where he began investigating the structure and evolution of stars.
majorContributions: Chandrasekhar's most famous achievement was the discovery of the Chandrasekhar Limit, which established the maximum mass a white dwarf star can possess before collapsing under its own gravity. This work revealed the pathways leading to neutron stars and black holes. He also made landmark contributions to stellar structure, radiative transfer, hydrodynamic stability, gravitational dynamics, and black hole theory. His mathematical approach brought exceptional rigor to astrophysics and influenced generations of researchers.
laterLife: Chandrasekhar spent most of his career at the University of Chicago, where he became one of the world's leading theoretical astrophysicists. He authored numerous influential books covering topics from stellar dynamics to general relativity. In 1983 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for his theoretical studies of the physical processes important to the structure and evolution of stars. His later work on black holes became a cornerstone of modern relativistic astrophysics.
whyImportant: Chandrasekhar fundamentally changed how scientists understand stars and their ultimate fate. His discoveries explained how massive stars evolve into white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes and helped establish many of the foundations of modern astrophysics. Today, every study of stellar evolution, compact objects, and black hole formation builds upon principles he developed.
